pr_title: gh-104357: fix inlined comprehensions that close over iteration var
pr_body:
This fixes the case where an inlined comprehension has an internal cellvar (i.e. it creates lambdas that close over the comprehension iteration variable), but the same name is also used a fast-local in the outer scope, and is read but never written within the body of the function (so e.g. an argument).

In code like this:

```
def f(x):
    items = [lambda: x for x in range(2)]
    return x
```

because `x` is a cell inside the comprehension, after inlining it would appear in `u_cellvars` for `f`, and thus the compilation of `f` would insert a `MAKE_CELL` for `x` at the start of the function. But we would still compile the non-comprehension part of the function treating `x` as a fast-local (emitting `LOAD_FAST` for it), so `f` would return a cell object containing the value of `x`, instead of returning `x` directly.

Similar cases were already tested, but only with a write (compiled as `STORE_FAST`) to `x` before it was referenced, which stored the value directly and overwrote the wrongly-created cell.

One approach to fix this would be to track which names are cells only inside an inlined comprehension, and prevent the compiler from emitting `MAKE_CELL` for those names (the inlined comprehension will itself emit `MAKE_CELL` where it should, within the comprehension's isolated scope.) But this fix would add additional complexity to the compiler.

A simpler fix (implemented here) is to ensure that we always treat such a variable as a cell throughout the outer function too (emitting `LOAD_DEREF` and `STORE_DEREF` for it). This maintains clearer semantics for `co_cellvars` (if a name is in there, it is a cell in the main function) and keeps the compiler simpler. The downside is that cells are slightly slower than fast locals, but comprehensions creating lambdas that close over the iteration variable are rare in real code (they don't behave as people usually want them to, given that all the created lambda functions share the same final value in their closure), so I don't think performance is a concern in this edge case.

Fixes #104357

issue_context.title: Comprehension inlining: Bug if comprehension contains a lambda
issue_context.body:
Code sample:

```python
def outer(x):
    return [lambda: x for x in range(x)]

print([f() for f in outer(2)])
```

On 3.11, this produces `[1, 1]` as expected.

But on current main, I get:

```
>>> [f() for f in outer(2)]
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "<stdin>", line 2, in outer
TypeError: 'cell' object cannot be interpreted as an integer
```

Almost certainly due to PEP 709 / #101441, cc @carljm.

comments:
Thanks for finding this case! I had tests for similar cases with lambda inside the comprehension using the same name as non-cell outside the comprehension, but they were all of the form:

```
def outer():
    x = 2
    return [lambda: x for x in range(x)]
```

The key factor in your example is that there is no store to `x` in the outer scope, because it is an argument.

review_comments: Could you explicitly test that the value of `x` is not clobbered after the comprehension? Something like the test below, but returning both `x` and the result of the listcomp. This would guard against a possible bug where the two cells are shared and the listcomp's cell overwrites the outer function's cell.
I think the existing `test_inner_cell_shadows_outer_redefined` test already protects against that possible bug?

The test I've added here does return both `x` and the result of the comprehension, but it returns `x` first. I could swap the order (`return [...], x` instead of `return x, [...]`), which would give confirmation from this test also that the comprehension isn't clobbering the outer `x`?
That one seems a little different because it contains a write to the variable in the outer scope, and that evidently makes a difference.
The test as it looks in the PR only returns the listcomp, not x. Agree that `return [...], x` would work for what I'm asking for.

Ah, right, I had experimented with a local change to the test, sorry :) I'll push the updated version that I described.

The presence of a write makes a difference for whether the "not treating it as a cell" previous code would be visibly broken or not by the initial `MAKE_CELL`, but now that it is treated as a cell, the presence or absence of write doesn't make any difference to the isolation. But there's certainly no harm in having both tests verify the isolation.
